cards.title: A model only does one thing
cards.body: Every chat model does exactly one move: guess the next token, add it, repeat. Code, essays, jokes, all of it is that loop running thousands of times.
cards.kicker: Next time an answer streams in, you're watching the loop live.

cards.title: Tokens aren't words
cards.body: A token is a chunk of text, often part of a word. 'Unbelievable' might be 3 tokens. Roughly, 1,000 tokens is about 750 English words.
cards.kicker: That's why limits and prices are counted in tokens, not words.

cards.title: Embeddings: words as directions
cards.body: Models turn each token into a long list of numbers, a point in a space with thousands of dimensions. Similar meanings land near each other.
cards.kicker: Famous trick: king minus man plus woman lands close to queen.

cards.title: Attention, in one picture
cards.body: Each word asks every earlier word 'are you relevant to me?' and blends in the answers. In 'the engine seized because it overheated', attention links 'it' back to 'engine'.
cards.kicker: That one mechanism is the T in GPT.

cards.title: Training vs inference
cards.body: Training sets the billions of numbers once, using huge amounts of text and compute. Inference is just using those frozen numbers to answer you.
cards.kicker: Your chat never changes the model's weights.

cards.title: Why models 'hallucinate'
cards.body: A model always produces the most likely-sounding next token, even when it doesn't actually know. Confident and wrong look the same from the inside.
cards.kicker: Fix: give it the real source (docs, files) in context, or let it search.

cards.title: Agents = model + tools + loop
cards.body: An agent is a model that can call tools (read a file, run a command), see the result, and decide the next step, over and over until done.
cards.kicker: Claude Code is an agent; the model inside it is the brain, the harness is the body.

cards.title: Context is the whole game
cards.body: A model only knows what's in its context window right now, plus what it learned in training. Good results mostly come from giving it the right context.
cards.kicker: That's why CLAUDE.md files and clear specs make agents way better.

cards.title: Temperature
cards.body: Temperature controls how random the next-token pick is. Low = predictable and repetitive. High = creative and sometimes unhinged.
cards.kicker: For code you want low; for brainstorming game ideas, higher.

cards.title: Fine-tuning vs prompting
cards.body: Prompting changes what you say to the model. Fine-tuning changes the model itself with extra training on your examples.
cards.kicker: Most apps never need fine-tuning: a good prompt plus the right context wins.

cards.title: RAG in one line
cards.body: Retrieval-augmented generation: search your own docs first, paste the best chunks into the prompt, then ask. The model answers from your stuff.
cards.kicker: A 'chat with my manual' app for your mechanic work would be RAG.

cards.title: RLHF: how chatbots learn manners
cards.body: After pretraining, people rank model answers, and the model is trained to prefer the higher-ranked style. That's a big part of why assistants feel helpful.
cards.kicker: Raw pretrained models just continue text; they don't 'answer'.

cards.title: Scaling laws
cards.body: Bigger models trained on more data with more compute get predictably better, along a smooth curve. That predictability is why companies spend billions.
cards.kicker: Welch Labs has a great video on this in the feed.

cards.title: Run models on your own PC
cards.body: Open-weight models can run locally on a good GPU with tools like Ollama or LM Studio. Smaller 'quantized' versions squeeze into less video memory.
cards.kicker: Rule of thumb: VRAM decides which model sizes you can run.

cards.title: Quantization
cards.body: Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits (like 4-bit instead of 16-bit) makes it much smaller and faster, losing a little quality.
cards.kicker: It's how big models fit on a gaming GPU.

cards.title: Diffusion: art from noise
cards.body: Image models start with pure static and remove noise step by step, steered by your text prompt, until a picture appears.
cards.kicker: Same idea now powers AI video.

cards.title: MCP: plugs for AI
cards.body: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way to give an AI tools and data, like a USB port. Your Silk Boards board talks to Claude through it.
cards.kicker: Build one MCP server and every MCP-aware app can use it.

cards.title: Interpretability
cards.body: Researchers look inside models to find 'features', directions in the numbers that mean things like 'Golden Gate Bridge' or 'code bug'.
cards.kicker: Turning a feature up or down actually changes how the model behaves.

cards.title: Mixture of experts
cards.body: Some big models are split into many 'experts' and only a few run for each token. Huge total size, but each answer only uses a slice.
cards.kicker: That's how some models are giant yet still fast.

cards.title: Reasoning models
cards.body: Newer models can 'think' in hidden tokens before answering. More thinking costs more tokens but cracks harder problems.
cards.kicker: That's the 'effort' setting you see in some tools.

cards.title: Light takes time
cards.body: Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it hits you. Light from the nearest star past the Sun left it over 4 years ago.
cards.kicker: Looking far away is looking back in time.

cards.title: GPS needs relativity
cards.body: Satellite clocks run fast by about 38 microseconds a day: weaker gravity speeds them up more than their speed slows them down. Without correcting it, GPS would drift several miles a day.
cards.kicker: Einstein is in your phone's map app.

cards.title: Quantum tunneling
cards.body: Tiny particles can pass through barriers they don't have the energy to climb over, because they behave like spread-out waves.
cards.kicker: The Sun only shines because protons tunnel close enough to fuse.

cards.title: Entropy is just counting
cards.body: There are vastly more messy arrangements than neat ones, so things drift toward messy. That's the second law of thermodynamics.
cards.kicker: It's also why your shop never cleans itself.

cards.title: Why the sky is blue
cards.body: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more than red ones, so blue light comes at you from every direction.
cards.kicker: Sunsets go orange because the light crosses so much air the blue gets scattered away.

cards.title: E = mc²
cards.body: A tiny bit of mass holds a huge amount of energy because c² is enormous. One gram of mass is roughly the energy of a 20-kiloton bomb.
cards.kicker: Nuclear power runs on turning a sliver of mass into heat.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.body: Before it's measured, a quantum particle isn't secretly in one state; its description is a mix of possibilities that can interfere with each other.
cards.kicker: Quantum computers exploit that interference to do certain math faster.

cards.title: Torque, the physics way
cards.body: Torque is force times the distance from the pivot. Double the wrench length and you get double the twist for the same push.
cards.kicker: A breaker bar is just physics you can hold.

cards.title: Why engines need gears
cards.body: An engine makes useful power only in a band of RPM. Gears trade speed for torque so the engine stays in that band from a stop to highway speed.
cards.kicker: First gear: lots of torque, little speed. Top gear: the reverse.

cards.title: Absolute zero
cards.body: At −273.15 °C, particles would have the least motion physics allows. You can get within billionths of a degree but never reach it.
cards.kicker: Labs do this to make atoms act like one giant quantum wave.

cards.title: Neutron stars
cards.body: A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball about the size of a city. A teaspoon would weigh billions of tons.
cards.kicker: Some spin hundreds of times a second.

cards.title: Black holes evaporate
cards.body: Hawking showed black holes slowly leak radiation and shrink. A big one would take far longer than the current age of the universe.
cards.kicker: Kurzgesagt's black hole video in the feed covers the whole life story.

cards.title: The universe is speeding up
cards.body: Distant galaxies are flying apart faster over time. Whatever pushes that is called dark energy, and nobody knows what it is.
cards.kicker: New surveys hint it might even be changing.

cards.title: Most of the universe is invisible
cards.body: Ordinary matter (atoms, stars, you) is only about 5% of everything. The rest is dark matter and dark energy.
cards.kicker: We know dark matter is there because galaxies spin too fast without it.

cards.title: Days on Venus
cards.body: Venus turns so slowly that its day is longer than its year, and it spins backwards compared to most planets.
cards.kicker: Sunrise there is in the west.

cards.title: Your brain runs on ~20 watts
cards.body: The human brain uses about as much power as a dim light bulb, while training a big AI model can use as much electricity as hundreds or even thousands of homes use in a year.
cards.kicker: Nature still wins on efficiency.

cards.title: Gödel in one breath
cards.body: In any math system rich enough to do arithmetic, there are true statements it can never prove.
cards.kicker: Veritasium's 'Math's Fundamental Flaw' is the long version.

cards.title: Game theory: tit for tat
cards.body: In repeated prisoner's dilemma tournaments, a simple strategy won: cooperate first, then copy what the other player did last time.
cards.kicker: Be nice, retaliate, forgive, be clear.

cards.title: Code tip: one change, then test
cards.body: Agents and people both break less when each change is small and checked before the next one. Big-bang changes hide the bug.
cards.kicker: Same as wrenching: swap one part, then start it.

cards.title: Git worktrees
cards.body: A worktree lets one repo have several folders checked out on different branches at once. Agents can work on two cards side by side without stepping on each other.
cards.kicker: Handy with several Claude sessions running.

cards.title: Tailscale in one line
cards.body: Tailscale builds a private network between your devices, so your phone reaches your PC at a fixed 100.x address from anywhere.
cards.kicker: It's how your launcher talks to Gibber Hub.

cards.title: PWA = website that installs
cards.body: A progressive web app has a manifest and a service worker, so the browser can install it with its own icon and run it full screen, even offline.
cards.kicker: This feed is one.
